## 3.2 Data analysis and model comparison

### Data preparation

The Aidlab pulse files contain heart rate in beats per minute and timestamps in Unix milliseconds. We convert the timestamps to minutes since each recording began. We retain the original time gaps and do not interpolate missing observations. Because the recordings do not provide labelled recovery start and end times, we analyse the falling-heart-rate interval visible in each supplied recording.

```{r}
library(minpack.lm)
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)
```

```{r}
find_repo_root <- function(start = getwd()) {
  path <- normalizePath(start, winslash = "/", mustWork = TRUE)

  repeat {
    if (file.exists(file.path(path, "IEAP-Series04-RStudio.qmd"))) {
      return(path)
    }

    parent <- dirname(path)
    if (identical(parent, path)) {
      stop("Could not find the repository root.")
    }
    path <- parent
  }
}

repo_root <- find_repo_root()

read_pulse <- function(folder_name) {
  file_path <- file.path(repo_root, "data", folder_name, "pulse.csv")
  pulse <- read.csv(file_path)

  if (!all(c("timestamp", "value") %in% names(pulse))) {
    stop(paste("Expected timestamp and value columns in", file_path))
  }

  pulse$timestamp <- as.numeric(pulse$timestamp)
  pulse$value <- as.numeric(pulse$value)
  pulse <- pulse[complete.cases(pulse[, c("timestamp", "value")]), ]
  pulse <- pulse[order(pulse$timestamp), ]

  pulse$time_min <- (pulse$timestamp - min(pulse$timestamp)) / 60000
  pulse$hr_bpm <- pulse$value

  pulse[, c("time_min", "hr_bpm")]
}

pulse_3h <- read_pulse("cardio_recovery_3h10m")
pulse_7m <- read_pulse("cardio_recovery_7m30s")

pulse_3h$recording <- "Three-hour recording"
pulse_7m$recording <- "7.5-minute recording"
pulse_all <- rbind(pulse_3h, pulse_7m)

kable(
  data.frame(
    Recording = c("Three-hour recording", "7.5-minute recording"),
    Observations = c(nrow(pulse_3h), nrow(pulse_7m)),
    Duration_minutes = c(
      round(max(pulse_3h$time_min), 2),
      round(max(pulse_7m$time_min), 2)
    ),
    First_HR_bpm = c(pulse_3h$hr_bpm[1], pulse_7m$hr_bpm[1]),
    Last_HR_bpm = c(tail(pulse_3h$hr_bpm, 1), tail(pulse_7m$hr_bpm, 1))
  ),
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Pulse data included in the analysis"
)
```
The three-hour recording contains 2,456 pulse observations over approximately 190 minutes. Heart rate falls from 130 bpm at the first observation to 64 bpm at the last. The 7.5-minute recording contains 91 observations over approximately 7.4 minutes, with heart rate falling from 155 to 129 bpm. Both recordings therefore show a decrease in heart rate across the observed period, but they differ greatly in duration, number of observations, and starting heart rate. We use the timestamps to preserve the recordings’ actual time scale, including any gaps. These summary values describe the recorded intervals; because the datasets do not label the exact start and end of recovery, they do not by themselves identify the full physiological recovery period.


### Observed heart rate over time

```{r q32-observed-plot, fig-cap="Observed heart rate in the two Aidlab recordings"}
ggplot(pulse_all, aes(x = time_min, y = hr_bpm)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ recording, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(
    x = "Time since recording began (minutes)",
    y = "Heart rate (bpm)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
Both recordings show an overall decrease in heart rate, but their patterns differ. In the 7.5-minute recording, heart rate falls quickly at first and then fluctuates around a slower decline. In the three-hour recording, heart rate also drops quickly early on, followed by a longer, noisy decline. These patterns suggest that a straight-line model may not capture the changing rate of decline well; we compare the fitted models next.

The datasets do not label the exact end of exercise or the start of recovery. We therefore use the recorded falling-heart-rate intervals as the available post-exercise recovery periods: from the beginning to the end of each pulse recording. This is an approximation, especially for the three-hour recording, which covers a much longer transition from effort toward rest. The fitted models describe these observed intervals, not a precisely identified recovery phase.


### Model fitting and numerical comparison

We fit a linear model, a mono-exponential decay, and a bi-exponential decay. The exponential models estimate an asymptotic heart rate. We compare AICc, RMSE, explained variance, model coefficients, and residual plots. A lower AICc and RMSE indicate a better statistical fit in this comparison, but model choice also depends on residual structure, complexity, and plausible parameter estimates.

```{r q32-models, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
fit_recovery_models <- function(data, recording_name) {
  data <- data[order(data$time_min), ]

  if (nrow(data) < 8) {
    stop(paste(recording_name, "has too few observations for model fitting."))
  }

  hr_start <- max(data$hr_bpm, na.rm = TRUE)
  hr_end <- median(
    tail(data$hr_bpm, max(3, floor(nrow(data) * 0.1))),
    na.rm = TRUE
  )
  amplitude <- max(1, hr_start - hr_end)

  linear <- lm(hr_bpm ~ time_min, data = data)

  mono <- nlsLM(
    hr_bpm ~ C + A * exp(-k * time_min),
    data = data,
    start = list(C = hr_end, A = amplitude, k = 0.1),
    lower = c(C = 30, A = 0, k = 0.00001),
    upper = c(C = hr_start, A = 250, k = 10),
    control = nls.lm.control(maxiter = 2000)
  )

  bi <- tryCatch(
    nlsLM(
      hr_bpm ~ C + A1 * exp(-k1 * time_min) + A2 * exp(-k2 * time_min),
      data = data,
      start = list(
        C = hr_end,
        A1 = 0.65 * amplitude,
        k1 = 0.5,
        A2 = 0.35 * amplitude,
        k2 = 0.05
      ),
      lower = c(C = 30, A1 = 0, k1 = 0.00001, A2 = 0, k2 = 0.00001),
      upper = c(C = hr_start, A1 = 250, k1 = 10, A2 = 250, k2 = 10),
      control = nls.lm.control(maxiter = 4000)
    ),
    error = function(e) NULL
  )

  models <- list(
    Linear = linear,
    `Mono-exponential` = mono
  )
  if (!is.null(bi)) {
    models$`Bi-exponential` <- bi
  }

  statistics <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(models), function(model_name) {
    model <- models[[model_name]]
    predicted <- as.numeric(predict(model, newdata = data))
    residual <- data$hr_bpm - predicted
    n <- nrow(data)
    parameter_count <- length(coef(model))
    aic <- AIC(model)

    aicc <- if (n > parameter_count + 1) {
      aic + (2 * parameter_count * (parameter_count + 1)) /
        (n - parameter_count - 1)
    } else {
      NA_real_
    }

    data.frame(
      recording = recording_name,
      model = model_name,
      RMSE_bpm = sqrt(mean(residual^2)),
      R_squared = 1 - sum(residual^2) /
        sum((data$hr_bpm - mean(data$hr_bpm))^2),
      AICc = aicc
    )
  }))

  diagnostics <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(models), function(model_name) {
    model <- models[[model_name]]
    predicted <- as.numeric(predict(model, newdata = data))

    data.frame(
      time_min = data$time_min,
      observed_hr = data$hr_bpm,
      predicted_hr = predicted,
      residual = data$hr_bpm - predicted,
      model = model_name,
      recording = recording_name
    )
  }))

  list(
    models = models,
    statistics = statistics,
    diagnostics = diagnostics
  )
}

results_3h <- fit_recovery_models(pulse_3h, "Three-hour recording")
results_7m <- fit_recovery_models(pulse_7m, "7.5-minute recording")

model_comparison <- rbind(
  results_3h$statistics,
  results_7m$statistics
)

kable(
  model_comparison,
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Numerical comparison of the fitted models"
)

# Print model coefficients so the estimated decay rates and asymptotes
# can be reported and assessed for plausibility.
cat("Three-hour recording model coefficients:\n")
print(lapply(results_3h$models, coef))

cat("\n7.5-minute recording model coefficients:\n")
print(lapply(results_7m$models, coef))
```

In the three-hour recording, the linear model estimates a decline of about 0.30 bpm per minute. The mono-exponential model estimates a faster initial decline that slows over time, approaching an asymptotic heart rate of about 64 bpm. The bi-exponential model estimates two decline rates, but its asymptote is about 42 bpm, well below the last observed heart rate of 64 bpm, so that long-term estimate may be unreliable.

In the 7.5-minute recording, the linear model estimates a decline of about 2.54 bpm per minute. The mono-exponential model approaches about 130 bpm, close to the final observed value of 129 bpm. The bi-exponential fit estimates an asymptote near 30 bpm, which is far below the observed range; this suggests its parameters may be poorly determined for this short recording.


### Fitted curves and residual analysis

```{r q32-fitted-curves, fig-cap="Observed heart rate and fitted models for each recording"}
diag_all <- rbind(
  results_3h$diagnostics,
  results_7m$diagnostics
)

ggplot(diag_all, aes(x = time_min)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = observed_hr), colour = "grey45", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(
    aes(y = predicted_hr, colour = model),
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ recording, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(
    x = "Time since recording began (minutes)",
    y = "Heart rate (bpm)",
    colour = "Model"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
In both recordings, the bi-exponential curve follows the observed decline more closely than the linear curve, which cannot represent the changing rate of decline. The fitted curves are similar for the 7.5-minute recording, so the comparison statistics and residuals are needed to judge whether the more complex model is justified.


```{r q32-residuals, fig-cap="Residuals over time for each fitted model"}
ggplot(diag_all, aes(x = time_min, y = residual)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.35, size = 0.7) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_grid(recording ~ model, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(
    x = "Time since recording began (minutes)",
    y = "Observed minus predicted heart rate (bpm)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
Residuals for the 7.5-minute recording are generally centred around zero. In the three-hour recording, residuals show more variation and some visible patterns, so even the best-fitting model does not capture every fluctuation. This is a limitation of the fit, particularly given the recording’s noise and gaps.


### Lowest-AICc model

```{r q32-best-models}
best_models <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(split(model_comparison, model_comparison$recording), function(x) {
    x <- x[!is.na(x$AICc), ]
    x[which.min(x$AICc), ]
  })
)

kable(
  best_models[, c("recording", "model", "AICc", "RMSE_bpm", "R_squared")],
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Lowest-AICc model in each recording"
)
```

The bi-exponential model had the lowest AICc in both recordings, so it was the best-supported model among those tested. Its RMSE was 3.114 bpm for the 7.5-minute recording and 7.944 bpm for the three-hour recording. The higher error in the longer recording reflects its noisier, more variable data; model choice should also consider the residual plots and whether the fitted parameters are physiologically plausible.
